name: Uma Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. My alarm goes at quarter past four and I'm in the parlour by half four, putting the clusters on 180 cows with Wojtek, who's been milking here twenty years and still corrects how I hold the teat dip. After milking it's scraping the yard, feeding calves, and whatever the boss, Mr Henderson, shouts across the yard. I like the calves best. What wears me out is the second milking at three, when your back's already gone and it's dark by half four in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And where do you live, in relation to the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In the tied cottage at the end of the lane, which means the house comes with the job. My partner Tomas drives a delivery van for the builders' merchant in town. We pay low rent, which is the only reason we get by, because I'm on the lower end of pay and I've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like now. Mr Henderson's got an app that tells him which cow's coming into heat, and that's about the size of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the cows still need milking and nobody's computer is going to stand in the slurry for you. At the pub I'd probably have a go at the tech people for all the fuss. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something rude about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but I'd also know it doesn't fix anything. Milk price is still set by the big processor, my pay is still low, and the cottage still belongs to the job. AI being a flop just means the old problems stay the old problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, milking and learning off Wojtek. I'd try to put twenty pounds a week aside from January, though I've said that every year. Maybe I'd finally go to one of the farmworkers' union meetings in town that Tomas keeps nagging me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, like being told the storm missed you but the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union meetings. What stops you going now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're on a Thursday night and I'm in bed by nine. And I suppose I've never had a reason that felt urgent. In this picture I still wouldn't, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you worry about most in a normal year like this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van. Not mine, Tomas's, because he has to keep it running himself and last winter the clutch went and it was £600. We put it on a card and we're still paying it off.

S0.say: I'd tell people the cows still need milking and nobody's computer is going to stand in the slurry for you. I'd have a go at the tech people for all the fuss.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix anything. The milk price is still set by the big processor, my pay stays low and the cottage still comes with the job.
S0.do: Keeps milking and learning from the senior herdsman. Tries again to save twenty pounds a week from January and might go to a union meeting, though she admits she probably won't.
S0.feel: Calm but flat, like being told a storm missed you while the roof still leaks.
S0.quote: AI being a flop just means the old problems stay the old problems.
S0.fieldNote: Uma's first instinct is to defend the physical work, but her real worries are older than AI: low pay, a processor that sets the milk price, and a house tied to the job. The tied cottage came up within the first minute and will matter a lot later. She is honest that she wouldn't act on the union idea unless pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but not a revolution. Okay. So robots in the parlour, then. That's already happening on the big units.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a robot can't tell when a cow's off her feed by the look in her eye, which is something Wojtek taught me. With friends I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates the companies selling this stuff. Online I'd share the union's posts about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think Mr Henderson would put in milking robots the first year he can get a grant for them. Robot units need one person to watch the screens, and that person would be Wojtek, not me. I'm the junior, I'm the cheap one, and I'm also the one who's slow with the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time I would actually go to the union meeting, the Thursday one. I'd ask Mr Henderson straight out whether he's looking at robots, because I'd rather know in March than find out from the delivery lorry. And I'd start looking at what Tomas's work would pay if I went on the yard there, which isn't much, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing a noise downstairs at night. Probably nothing, but you lie there listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Wojtek would keep the job, not you. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't blame him. He's got two kids and he knows more about cows than the robot company ever will. I'd blame the people who decided a grant for a robot is a better use of public money than paying a person properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to learn the robot system to stay, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but I'd be bad at it, I know that. I've never used one of those chat things and I'm slow on the parlour computer as it is. It would take someone patient sitting next to me, and on a farm nobody has time to be patient.

S1.say: I'd say a robot can't tell when a cow's off her feed by the look in her eye. With friends I'd blame the lack of rules on the companies selling the machines, and I'd share the union's posts.
S1.think: I think the boss would buy milking robots the first year a grant covers them. The one person kept to watch the screens would be the senior herdsman, not the cheap junior who's slow with the tablet.
S1.do: Goes to the farmworkers' union meeting and asks her boss directly in spring whether robots are coming. Starts checking what yard work at her partner's builders' merchant would pay as a fallback.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise downstairs at night and lying awake listening.
S1.quote: I'm the junior, I'm the cheap one, and I'm also the one who's slow with the tablet.
S1.fieldNote: Here the abstract worry turns into a clear picture: robot milkers, one screen-watcher, and Uma not being that person. She blames grant policy and unregulated companies rather than her boss or her colleague. She would act on the union idea now, but is frank that learning the robot system would be a struggle without patient support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I've even paid off the clutch. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud everywhere: this is a choice rich people made for the rest of us. At work I'd tell Mr Henderson he owes Wojtek and me more than a handshake. Online I'd be angry for once, properly angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I lose my job and my home in the same week. That's the bit people in cities don't get about tied cottages. If the robot milks the cows, the robot doesn't need the cottage. So Mr Henderson rents it out or knocks it down for a slurry store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop spending on anything that isn't food or diesel. I'd ask my mum if we could have her back bedroom if it came to it, which I'd hate. In the first year after, I'd sign up for whatever government help exists and I'd be on every union and protest list going, because with two years there's no time to train for anything, and I'm not a computer person anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in my stomach. I keep thinking about carrying boxes out of the cottage in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years change, compared with if it took longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. It's two calving seasons. With that little time you don't plan, you just brace. I couldn't save a deposit for a flat, I couldn't learn a trade, I couldn't even get Tomas's van paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night you knew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to my mum's and it's not forever. And I'd probably cry, and he'd make tea, because that's what he does. Then I'd ask him if the van could be turned into a business, moving people's stuff, because there'd be a lot of people moving.

S2.say: I'd say everywhere that this is a choice rich people made for everyone else. I'd tell the boss he owes the workers more than a handshake and, for once, be openly angry online.
S2.think: I think I'd lose my job and my home in the same week, because the cottage is tied to the job. If a robot milks the cows, the boss doesn't need a worker in the cottage.
S2.do: Cuts spending to food and diesel immediately and asks her mother about moving into her back bedroom. After the change, signs up for government help and joins every union and protest action she can.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick to her stomach, picturing carrying boxes out of the cottage in the rain.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. It's two calving seasons. With that little time you don't plan, you just brace.
S2.fieldNote: The tied cottage turns a job threat into a housing threat, and that doubled loss is what drives her alarm. With two years she sees no route to retraining, so her plan is all defence: cut spending, family, state help, protest. Her one spark of initiative was turning her partner's van into a moving business, which she raised almost as a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit different, isn't it. Not a lot, but a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about who chose this, but I'd also be telling people at the union to use the five years, not waste it shouting. I'd want proper rules: if a farm gets a grant for robots, the workers get paid out and get help finding a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I could do something, but I know myself. I'd drag my feet for three of them and then panic. I'm not proud of that. The bit that changes is the cottage: in five years Tomas and I could maybe save enough to rent somewhere that isn't tied to anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd make saving the cottage problem the main thing: fifty pounds a week into a separate account, no touching it. I'd ask the union about any course for farm workers, maybe the large animal vet nurse course at the college, because the robots still need someone when a cow's actually ill. Then once it arrived, I'd hope I was already halfway out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a different anxious. More like exam nerves than being chased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet. What would get you moving earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody I trust doing it first. If Wojtek went on a course and said it was fine, I'd go. Or if the union set it up and I was sat in a room with other milkers my age, not teenagers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're saving fifty a week in this picture but twenty felt hard in the first one. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. Twenty is what I can do when I'm not scared. Fifty is what I'd do when I'm scared. Fear's a good accountant. I'd have to cut the takeaways and Tomas's football.

S3.say: I'd say the same about who chose this, but tell the union to use the five years instead of only shouting. I'd want rules that pay workers out and help them find a home when a farm gets a robot grant.
S3.think: Five years means I could do something, but I'd likely drag my feet and then panic. The real change is that we could save enough to rent somewhere not tied to the job.
S3.do: Saves fifty pounds a week into a separate account to get out of the tied cottage. Asks the union about courses, such as a large-animal vet nurse course at the local college.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more like exam nerves than being chased.
S3.quote: Twenty is what I can do when I'm not scared. Fifty is what I'd do when I'm scared. Fear's a good accountant.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts Uma from bracing to planning, and her first plan is about housing, not career. She admits her own resistance to change and names what would overcome it: a trusted person going first or a union-run course with her peers. She accepted the contradiction about saving with good humour and a sharp line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Huh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do this properly, so there's no excuse. At work I'd be pushing for a plan, written down, for what happens to the people on this farm. Online I'd be sharing the union's petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years scares me in a sneaky way. It's long enough that I'd tell myself it's ages away, and short enough that it isn't. I'd be 37 with nothing to show for it except that I can milk a cow, which by then a machine can do too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd do the vet nurse course part-time, even if it took three years instead of one. I'd get us out of the tied cottage by year five, so the house and the job aren't the same thing anymore. And I'd go to the union every month, because with ten years you can actually change the rules, not just complain about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. There's room to breathe, but I don't trust myself to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to be in charge of that ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the robot companies, that's for sure. The government and the unions, with farmers in the room. Mr Henderson's not a bad man, but he'll do what the bank tells him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your 37-year-old self to have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A front door that's mine, even if it's rented. A skill a machine doesn't do yet. And a few months of money, which sounds like nothing but I've never had it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for the government to handle this properly, so there's no excuse. I'd push for a written plan for the farm's workers and share the union's petitions.
S4.think: Ten years scares me in a sneaky way: long enough to tell myself it's ages away, short enough that it isn't. I'd be 37 and the only thing I can do, a machine could do too.
S4.do: Starts a part-time vet nurse course within two years and moves out of the tied cottage by year five. Goes to monthly union meetings to push for rules while there is time to change them.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, with room to breathe but little trust in herself to use it.
S4.quote: It's long enough that I'd tell myself it's ages away, and short enough that it isn't.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is the only picture where Uma sees politics as able to change the outcome, not just protest it. Her plan is the same as in the five-year picture, stretched out, which suggests the course and the move are her real fallback. She keeps returning to the same three wants: a home that isn't tied, one skill, and a few months saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and I lose the job and the cottage together, and I've got no money to land on. What would help is a law that says if your home comes with the job, you can't be put out for at least a year after the job goes, and someone paid to sit with people like me and teach us something new slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everybody talks about the workers, but nobody's asked what a farm's like when nobody knows the cows by name. Maybe that sounds soft. I'd still like someone to ask it.

headlineQuote: If the robot milks the cows, the robot doesn't need the cottage.
portrait: Uma Petrov is a 27-year-old junior dairy worker who milks 180 cows twice a day and lives with her partner Tomas in a cottage that comes with the job. She has about three weeks of savings, has never used an AI tool and knows she's slow with new technology. She blames grant policy, big processors and unregulated tech companies rather than her boss. In the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption pictures she mostly hangs on, but in the AGI pictures her fear is losing her job and her home at once. More warning time moves her from bracing and leaning on family to a real plan: a vet nurse course, savings and a move out of the tied cottage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she would lose her job and her tied cottage together with no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A law that protects people in job-linked homes for at least a year after the job goes, and patient, paid help to learn a new skill slowly.
